explanations.answer: He blesses the people in the name of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. When David finishes sacrificing the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blesses the people in the name of the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:2). The offerings wrap up and good words go out over the people. I'd take a blessing over a plain old handshake any day.

explanations.answer: He reads the Law of Moses to the people
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible guess, but this verse doesn't have a scroll in it. It says David blessed the people in the name of the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:2). No reading is mentioned at this point. I'd probably have reached for a scroll too, friend, so you're in good company.

explanations.answer: He leads the people on a march through the city
explanations.explanation: No march here. The ark is already inside the tent, and after the offerings David blesses the people in the name of the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:2). The shouting and horns came earlier, as they brought the ark in (1 Chronicles 15:28). I bet everybody's feet were glad to stand still for a minute.

Not just the Levites, friend. The text says David distributed a loaf of bread, a date cake and a raisin cake to every man and woman of Israel (1 Chronicles 16:3). The Levites weren't the only ones getting a snack. Every man and woman of Israel was on that list.

That's right, it's FALSE. David gave a loaf of bread, a date cake and a raisin cake to every man and woman of Israel (1 Chronicles 16:3). The list wasn't just the Levites. That's how you throw a celebration.

Thanks it is. The Levites are appointed to celebrate, to give thanks and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel (1 Chronicles 16:4). All three jobs are pointed at the LORD. I'd take that job without even asking about the pay.

Orders sounds like a king's kind of job, but the verse doesn't say it. These Levites are to celebrate, to give thanks and to praise the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:4). It's a thank-you job, friend. No one's handing out clipboards here.

Warnings aren't in this verse. The job is to celebrate, to give thanks and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel (1 Chronicles 16:4). I think that's a much nicer job than standing around saying 'careful now.' This one is all thanks.

TRUE, baker. The song says, “let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice.” (1 Chronicles 16:10) It's the hearts of the seekers that get the call to rejoice. That's a song worth singing along to.

This one is actually true, friend. The song says, “let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice.” (1 Chronicles 16:10) I know, it sounded too easy to be true. I second-guess the easy ones myself, so no shame here.

That's it. The song calls, “O offspring of His servant Israel, O sons of Jacob, His chosen ones.” (1 Chronicles 16:13) Three ways of saying it, and every one points to the same family. When a call is said three times, you can bet it matters.

Close, since kings do show up in this song. But here the call goes to “O offspring of His servant Israel, O sons of Jacob, His chosen ones.” (1 Chronicles 16:13) The kings come in later, where the LORD rebukes them on behalf of the wanderers (1 Chronicles 16:21). Right song, different verse.

The elders aren't named in this part. The song calls “O offspring of His servant Israel, O sons of Jacob, His chosen ones.” (1 Chronicles 16:13) That's the whole family, not just a few leaders. It's a wide invitation, friend.

Not quite, baker. The song says, “He is the LORD our God; His judgments carry throughout the earth.” (1 Chronicles 16:14) Throughout the earth, not just Israel's backyard. That's a long way for anything to carry.
That's right, it's FALSE. The song says, “He is the LORD our God; His judgments carry throughout the earth.” (1 Chronicles 16:14) The song doesn't stop at Israel's border. It says the whole earth.

That's right, baker. In the song, God says to Jacob and Israel, ‘I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance.’ (1 Chronicles 16:18) It's a promise made as an inheritance. Notice it's land, not a thing you can put in your pocket.

No crown in this promise. The song says God would give them “…the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance.” (1 Chronicles 16:18) I know gold sounds fancy, friend. But the promise here is land, plain and simple.

Cedar's a fine wood, but it's not in this promise. The song says God would give them “…the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance.” (1 Chronicles 16:18) That's the inheritance named in the covenant. Nothing about a building here.

explanations.answer: He lets no one oppress them
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The song says, “He let no man oppress them…” (1 Chronicles 16:21) They were wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another (1 Chronicles 16:20). Wandering is hard enough, but they weren't wandering unwatched.

explanations.answer: He lets them fend for themselves
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what the song says. It says, “He let no man oppress them…” (1 Chronicles 16:21) The LORD stepped in for them while they wandered. They weren't left to fend for themselves, friend.

explanations.answer: He sends them into the desert
explanations.explanation: The song never says that. It says they wandered from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another (1 Chronicles 16:20). Then it says, “He let no man oppress them…” (1 Chronicles 16:21). The LORD's part in this verse is protecting them.

Kings is right. The song says of the LORD, “He rebuked kings on their behalf…” (1 Chronicles 16:21). Then the LORD says, ‘Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!’ (1 Chronicles 16:22) Even kings got told to keep their hands to themselves.

Priests are in this passage, but they're not the ones rebuked here. The verse says the LORD “…rebuked kings on their behalf…” (1 Chronicles 16:21). The priests Benaiah and Jahaziel are blowing trumpets before the ark in this chapter (1 Chronicles 16:6). Different job, friend.

Elders aren't the ones in this verse. It says, “He rebuked kings on their behalf…” (1 Chronicles 16:21). Then the LORD says, ‘Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!’ (1 Chronicles 16:22). The word you're looking for is kings.

explanations.answer: Other gods are idols but He made the heavens
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the song gives. “For all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens.” (1 Chronicles 16:26) On one side, idols. On the other, the One who made the heavens. That's a big gap, friend.

explanations.answer: Other gods are new but He was there first
explanations.explanation: That sounds nice, but the song doesn't say it. The reason it gives is, “For all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens.” (1 Chronicles 16:26) It's about idols on one side and the Maker of the heavens on the other. Nothing about who showed up first.

explanations.answer: Other gods are far but He is close by
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't use distance here. It says, “For all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens.” (1 Chronicles 16:26) That's the reason it gives for fearing Him above all gods. Idols on one side, the Maker of the heavens on the other.

Not only Israel, baker. The song says, “Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the nations, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength.” (1 Chronicles 16:28) It's calling the families of the nations. The invitation is a wide one.

That's right, it's FALSE. The song says, “Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the nations, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength.” (1 Chronicles 16:28) The families of the nations are called too. That's a big crowd, friend.
An offering is right. The song says, “bring an offering and come before Him.” (1 Chronicles 16:29) Nobody's told to show up empty-handed. It's a come-and-bring kind of invitation.

Idols aren't what the song says to bring. Just a few verses earlier it says, “For all the gods of the nations are idols…” (1 Chronicles 16:26). What it tells them to bring is, “bring an offering and come before Him.” (1 Chronicles 16:29) The thing it names is an offering, friend.

No swords in this invitation, friend. The song says, “bring an offering and come before Him.” (1 Chronicles 16:29) A sword would be a strange thing to carry into my bakery, and I'd have questions. The thing the song names to bring is an offering.

explanations.answer: He is coming to judge the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the reason in the song. “Then the trees of the forest will sing for joy before the LORD, for He is coming to judge the earth.” (1 Chronicles 16:33) The reason given is His coming. No tricks in this one, baker, you read it right.

explanations.answer: The long winter is finally over
explanations.explanation: I'd sing too if a long winter ended, but the song gives a different reason. It says the trees “…will sing for joy before the LORD, for He is coming to judge the earth.” (1 Chronicles 16:33) Nothing about seasons in this verse. The reason is His coming.

explanations.answer: The harvest has all come in
explanations.explanation: Harvest isn't mentioned here. The song says the trees “…will sing for joy before the LORD, for He is coming to judge the earth.” (1 Chronicles 16:33) That's the reason it gives. A full harvest would be nice, though.

TRUE, baker. The song says, “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.” (1 Chronicles 16:34) Earlier the song just said to give thanks (1 Chronicles 16:8). This time it comes with the reason.

Flip that one around, friend, because it's TRUE. This time the song gives the reason: give thanks to the LORD because He is good and His loving devotion endures forever (1 Chronicles 16:34). Back in verse 8 it just said to give thanks (1 Chronicles 16:8). I once stared at a finished batch for ten minutes asking myself if it was done, and the whole time my timer was going off.

explanations.answer: So they may give thanks to His holy name
explanations.explanation: That's it. The cry says, “…that we may give thanks to Your holy name, that we may glory in Your praise.” (1 Chronicles 16:35) The song ends up right back at thanks. It started there too.

explanations.answer: So they may rule over every nation
explanations.explanation: Ha, big dreams, friend! But that isn't in this cry. The people ask to be saved so that, in the song's words, “…that we may give thanks to Your holy name, that we may glory in Your praise.” (1 Chronicles 16:35) Thanks is the whole point there, not a crown. I can barely run my own counter, and it's only one counter.

explanations.answer: So they may build Him a great temple
explanations.explanation: A temple isn't mentioned in this cry. It says, “…that we may give thanks to Your holy name, that we may glory in Your praise.” (1 Chronicles 16:35) The reason given is thanks and praise. Hard hats can stay on the hook, friend.
TRUE, baker. The song ends, and then all the people said, “Amen!” and “…praise the LORD…” (1 Chronicles 16:36) The whole crowd answers back. That's a good way to close a song.

This one is actually true, friend. After the song, all the people said, “Amen!” and “…praise the LORD…” (1 Chronicles 16:36) The whole crowd answered together. I'd have been hollering right along with them, so don't sweat this one.

Bless is right. The people head to their homes, and David returns home to bless his household (1 Chronicles 16:43). He blessed the people at the start (1 Chronicles 16:2), and now he blesses his own household. I like a day that opens and closes with a blessing.
Teaching is a good thing, but it's not in this verse. David returns home “…to bless his household.” (1 Chronicles 16:43) That's how the chapter ends. The word you want is bless.

Gathering already happened, friend, and the crowd has headed home. David returns home “…to bless his household.” (1 Chronicles 16:43) The word is bless. He has one more stop to make, and it's his own front door.
